description: We are a team of IT students from Birzeit University with diverse technical skills and interests in technology, innovation, and problem-solving. We chose a NASA challenge focused on creating an educational game for children aged 7–12 about managing a lunar or Martian outpost and balancing essential resources. We welcome creative, collaborative team members with interests in programming, game development, UI/UX, graphic design, space science, and data visualization.
summary: Ready, Raed? is a free browser game for kids aged 7–12 that trains them to run a Moon base for five days. Players manage air, water, food and power, make oxygen from water, and rush astronaut Raed to a shelter when a real NASA solar storm, taken from the DONKI database, hits. No choice is free: water for plants means less to drink. Kids learn real space trade-offs by trying, failing and trying again. It needs no install, and it labels what is real and what is simplified.
details:
Ready, Raed? is a free, browser-based mission-trainer game for kids aged 7–12. Players run a Moon base for five days, helping astronaut Raed stay alive. They plan daily power, make air, water plants to grow food, and protect him from a solar storm. No choice is free: water for plants is water not to drink, and power for the shelter can't be used for air or plants. When a supply runs out, Raed loses a heart, and the report explains why. Kids learn by trying, failing and trying again.

Real NASA data drives the game. Players pick an actual solar event from the DONKI database (archived data, not live), such as the storm of 10 May 2024. A Mission Control message from Earth shows the real 1.3-second signal delay. The storm countdown is compressed: the real storm took about 6 hours, and the game gives seconds. Air and water use follow NASA life-support planning values (BVAD). The game labels what is simplified: power numbers, the storm countdown and a dice rule.

Impact: it makes real deep-space constraints (air, water, food, power, radiation) playable and understandable, so kids ask "why?" It needs no install and works on school computers. Next steps are testing with children, adding Arabic, more missions and Mars.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no backend), the Web Audio API for sounds, and NASA DONKI data saved as JSON.

Creativity: kids choose a real storm and make oxygen by splitting H₂O.
dataRefs: NASA Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (BVAD), life-support values
